doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Leaving Norvo for Claude Thornhill and the Schribman office
summary: He and Gozzo left Norvo for Thornhill at Glen Island with Schribman backing; swing bands compared to rock bands.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I loved parts of it. And when I first left home with the Dick Stabile scene, I was so homesick, but then I outgrew it. You know you’d get to be buddies with the guys you worked with, and they’re like a family. I roomed with Conrad for two and a half years. We left Red Norvo’s band to go with Claude Thornhill’s band. We left together. And then when we left several others, Barry Gallbraith and Ted Goddard and a few others from that great little band left, actually we broke up the band, which for the moment Red didn’t like us too well. And we left with Claude because Claude was going into Glen Island and the Schribman office was giving him the same build-up they gave — it didn’t have the same result — but Glenn Miller.
Boy I’ve heard that name a lot, Schribman.
Yes, yes. Sy Schribman and he had a brother. They were big in the New England area.
So if they got behind your big band you had a decent chance.

Yeah. At that time they were carrying microphones up to the stage all the time. And we recorded for Columbia. That was the beginning of Claude getting really into some kind of a public recognition. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

It’s hard to envision, I think for young people today with the rock & roll bands that tour today and so forth today, and record, that what you guys were doing, that was the scene. That the swing bands were like the rock & roll bands. Is that a fair statement?

I think so. Well when we would work theaters, like you worked the Paramount Theater, you would have like fans standing at the stage door for autographs and stuff. In that sense it was. There were parallels, yeah.
